projects.title: Mateo Weather Network
projects.tagline: Community weather stations for cities, farms, and off-grid valleys.
projects.summary: An open-source, solar-powered weather network designed to bring reliable local forecasts to areas that commercial stations miss.
projects.whatItSolves: Official weather stations cost thousands of dollars, while cheap backyard sensors give false readings whenever the sun hits them. Mateo pairs sub-$100 solar hardware with automatic neighbor cross-checking to filter out bad data.
highlights: Three station setups tailored for city balconies, rural farms, and off-grid villages
Automatic quality checks spot and ignore sudden temperature spikes
Solar-powered design that runs for months through cloudy weather

projects.title: RFID Student Access
projects.tagline: Local door access for classrooms and student workshops.
projects.summary: A self-hosted badge access system built on two separate ESP microcontrollers and a lightweight local web page—with zero recurring cloud fees.
projects.whatItSolves: Many all-in-one door readers put the lock relay right behind the exterior plastic cover where wires can be shorted. Splitting the reader (outside) from the lock switch (inside) keeps the room secure while running entirely on the building LAN.
highlights: Two-part hardware keeps the lock switch safely inside the room
Runs on your local network and keeps working if the internet drops
Simple browser page for adding student cards and viewing attendance

projects.title: Macro 3×3 Pad
projects.tagline: A 9-key shortcut pad that stores your bindings on the chip.
projects.summary: A compact 3×3 USB keypad that saves your custom shortcuts directly to onboard memory so you never have to leave configuration software running.
projects.whatItSolves: Most programmable keypads require bloated background apps and forget your shortcuts as soon as you plug them into another computer. Macro writes your 9 key combos straight to the microcontroller chip.
highlights: Program your keys once with a small Python utility, then close it
Shortcuts stay on the hardware chip across Windows, Mac, and Linux
Works immediately as a standard driverless USB keyboard
